chunks: Muhammad ibn Ibrahim ibn Ishaq al-Mu'addib - may God be pleased with him - narrated that Ahmad ibn Ali al-Ansari quoted on the authority of Abdul Salam ibn Salih al-Harawi, who said: I heard Abu al-Hasan Ali ibn Musa ibn Ja'far (peace be upon him) saying:
Whoever believes in predestination (al-jabr), do not give him from the alms-tax (zakat) and do not accept his testimony.
Indeed, God, the Blessed and Exalted, does not burden any soul beyond its capacity, nor does He load it above its power.
And every soul earns not [blame] except against itself, and no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another.

key_terms.الْجَبْر: Predestination (theological doctrine asserting God's absolute control over human actions)
key_terms.وِزْرَ أُخْرَىٰ: Burden of another (carrying the sins of others)

ai.seo_question: What is the Shia ruling on giving zakat to those who believe in divine predestination (al-jabr)?
ai.summary: In this tradition from Imam Ali ibn Musa al-Rida, the concept of 'al-jabr' (strict divine predestination denying human agency) is identified as a theological defect that disqualifies an individual from receiving Zakat and having their testimony accepted, reflecting the Shia emphasis on 'Amr bayn al-amrayn' (a position between absolute predestination and absolute free will). The Imam grounds this social and legal exclusion in Quranic principles of divine justice, specifically citing that God does not burden souls beyond their capacity and that each person bears only their own sins, thereby affirming human responsibility for their choices.
